articles.title: Meet Sumira Tiwari, who dreams of flying the Rafale and secured 11th rank in the NDA; one of only two women selected for the Indian Air Force's flying branch, she was inspired by wearing her father's helmet and boots
articles.summary: Sumira Tiwari is only 18, and she has already aimed higher in the sky than most of us dare to dream, and quite literally.
articles.body: Sumira Tiwari is only 18, and she has already aimed higher in the sky than most of us dare to dream, and quite literally. This year, the Lucknow teenager ranked 11th among the successful girls on the National Defence Academy merit list, and she is one of just two women picked for the Indian Air Force's flying branch.She is a daughter who grew up around Air Force stations, watching helicopters cross the sky, including inside her father's helicopter, and never forgot it. And today, through quiet, patient self-study and practice, she has made a name for herself too.Meet Sumira Tiwari, the Lucknow teen who bagged 11th rank in the NDA merit list following her father’s legacySumira Tiwari is an 18-year-old girl from Lucknow who secured the 11th rank in the merit list, following her father's legacy, and was selected into the Indian Air Force as one among the only two women who are selected for the Indian Air Force (IAF) flying branch.As a little girl, she loved to slip her tiny feet into her father's big flying boots, put on his uniform cap, and imagine herself flying an aircraft. Years later, that childhood fascination and relentless endeavour brought her a step closer to the cockpit of a fighter jet.According to a previous TOI report, Sumira lives in Vikas Nagar and is the elder daughter of retired Wing Commander Santosh Tiwari, who now works as a commercial pilot with a private helicopter charter company, and his wife, Shweta Tiwari. Her younger sister, Sumedha, who is 15, studies at City Montessori School, Gomti Nagar 1, the same school where Sumira completed her own schooling.Sumira grew up at different Air Force stations. She was fascinated by the helicopters flying overhead and by the stories her father told her about his flying missions.From wearing her father’s helmet to visiting the helicopter’s cockpit is what inspired her to dream of following in the footsteps of the IAF"The very first time I thought of wearing the blues as a pilot was when Papa showed us what his helicopter looked like from the inside," she recalledTrying on her father's night-vision helmet was another moment she still remembers. "I was awed. I think that's when this seed of wanting to fly got planted in my subconscious," she said.Getting into the NDA took Sumira nearly a year of preparation and several rounds of selection. She mostly studied on her own while also getting ready for her ISC board exams, and she attended a two-week SSB orientation programme in Lucknow.According to her, the hardest part was not the written exam or the six-day Services Selection Board (SSB) interview. It was the anxiety of waiting for the results at every stage. "The toughest part wasn't the vast syllabus or the exhausting SSB interview. The toughest part was the wait," she said.Her selection brought back memories of her father’s Air Force journeyHer selection has also brought back memories for her father, who went through the same route himself. "Her going to the Indian Air Force following the same route makes me very nostalgic. All the memories of 1994 come flooding into my mind as I visualise her joining the coveted National Defence Academy," Santidh said, calling it a homecoming.For her mother, the news has brought back something the family had been missing. "The blue had started fading in our lives after my husband separated from the IAF a few years back, and I am so happy that we will be deep in blue again," she said.She dreams of flying the RafaleHer father spent his flying career with helicopters, but Sumira has bigger plans. She wants to fly fighter jets, and she has one in particular in mind. "The Falcon of the Indian skies. The Dassault Rafale," she said.According to the UPSC results declared on Nov 5, Sumira ranked 11th among 66 successful female candidates. articles.title: Newfoundland: The Canadian province with the Irish accent
articles.summary: A new Netflix series features characters with an Irish accent in somewhere you might not expect to find it.
articles.body:
Watch 10 minutes of Netflix's horror mini-series Below and you'll likely be asking yourself: 'Why are they talking with Irish accents when it's in Canada?'

The series is set in a remote coastal fishing town in Newfoundland, Canada's most easterly province.

It follows fisherman Calvin Penney, played by Josh Hartnett, as a mysterious sea creature begins terrorising the community.

And while the main characters' "Irish" accents may seem out of place, Newfoundland has always been a place apart from the rest of Canada.

Fishing, specifically for cod, was what first brought the Irish - mainly from counties Waterford, Wexford, Kilkenny, Tipperary and Cork - to Newfoundland, as Willeen Keough of the Newfoundland Historical Society explains.

The Irish came in boats owned by people from the West Country of England who had established a fishery in Newfoundland and settled there.

"[The West Country fishermen] started to go to the south-east and south shore of Ireland to look for cheaper provisions and for labour for the fishery and that's how the Irish ended up coming out," Keough says.

"They started coming in the late 1600s, primarily though in the 1700s and up to the 1830s. They increasingly replaced English fishers."

She says the immigration "wasn't that kind of mad desperation that drove the later famine migrations".

"They were fishing servants, they were indentured servants coming out. They were paid but they were of that class and status."

While much of the original migration was seasonal, Keough says the Irish eventually settled in areas like the Avalon Peninsula.

"You've got from the Cape Shore around St Mary's Bay; the Southern Shore - a very, very Irish part of Newfoundland; St John's; and then moving into Conception Bay more mixed populations - but the Irish are also there as well.

"You can see that isolation and separation is part of the story there in terms of why Irish people didn't lose their language."

She adds: "Right at the moment I would say what you have is sort of a mélange or mix of West Country [English] and Irish but there are still very distinctive Irish undertones in certain areas.

"We have the d instead of the th - dis, dat and dose.

"The silent h in the thr combination - so instead of three people we'll say 'tree', or 'true' instead of through.

"The people who grew up on the shores, they have such a distinctively Irish sound.

"When they go to Ireland - because people do that these days - people won't believe that they're not Irish, it's that close."

Prof Raymond Hickey is a linguistics expert at the University of Limerick.

He says Newfoundland is an outlier. In the US, Australia and New Zealand, the Irish accent disappeared within a generation.

"The fact that they were isolated for such a long time, far away from the centre of Canada, meant they preserved whatever input they had both from south-west England and also south-east Ireland," he says.

While it became more diluted after Newfoundland became part of Canada in 1949, the Irish accent persists in parts of the province, says Hickey.

"Certainly still to this day in places like Tilting, or on what's called the southern shore, places near the Burin Peninsula - basically away from St John's, the capital, there would be considerable retention of Irish accents.

"I went up to Tilting once and I could have been in County Waterford the way people were talking.

"They use 'do be' which is very common: 'They do be out fishing.'

"Also the use of s on other parts of the present tense apart from the third person singular so: 'I gets up early in the morning', that sort of thing. Or: 'Lots of people does be there.'

Keough says there has been "a sort of cultural renaissance" in Newfoundland.

In the 1960s, '70s into the '80s, students recorded older people, capturing the distinctive accent.

"It reinforced the notion that this is not something to be ashamed of," says Keough.

"So we didn't get sucked into the combination accent of the mainland, we did remain kind of separate."

She says in the 1990s the Irish government and the Newfoundland government signed a memorandum of understanding

"Then there were all these moments of getting together for economic reasons, but also educational and academic and cultural moments.

"That really encouraged Irish [Newfoundland] people with an Irish dialect to keep it up.

"People genuinely wanted to hold on to it but it was reinforced by that and reinforced by tourism - that sort of sold the idea of the Irishness of Newfoundland.

"When people come over here from Ireland they are amazed. I think they feel a great deal of emotional attachment."

When Keough lived in British Columbia for a time, people would ask her if she was Irish.

"I would say no, but I am an Irish Newfoundlander and I would identify as that," she says.

"I think it's becoming a little more fashionable again."

articles.title: Low Carbon unveils plan for solar farms on Essex Dengie Peninsula
articles.summary: Low Carbon wants to install solar panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of Essex countryside.
articles.body:
Plans have been unveiled to build one of the biggest solar farms in the UK across a huge slice of Essex's Dengie Peninsula.

Low Carbon wants to install panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of sprawling countryside between Burnham-on-Crouch and Bradwell-on-Sea.

The developer said the site could generate 1GW of power - enough to supply 250,000 homes, or every house between Basildon and Shoeburyness.

However, critics have questioned how the project will impact wildlife and local roads during construction.

The scheme has been deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project, which means the government has the final say on whether it will go ahead.

Simon Morgan, the Conservative leader of Maldon District Council, said it had emerged "out of the blue".

"It was a complete shock when we saw the extent of the area that's being planned," he told the BBC.

"It's almost, in my view, one-third of the land in the Dengie Peninsula, which is quite an extensive amount of land to be put under solar panels."

Plans published online by Low Carbon showed seven potential sites have been earmarked for solar farms and battery energy storage systems.

They stretch from near the decommissioned Bradwell nuclear power station to Burnham-on-Crouch, passing Tillingham and Southminster.

In total, the land proposed for development is equivalent to about 2,400 football pitches. Low Carbon described it as one of the biggest solar farms in the UK.

"The scale of this has slightly knocked people sideways," said James Taylor, chairman of the Dengie Climate Action Partnership.

Taylor is torn between championing renewable energy and feeling concerned about how the site could impact wildlife, particularly as it is a crucial migration route for birds.

"It's an enormously important international area for wildlife and a Site of Special Scientific Interest," added Roger Morland, the chairman of Burnham Against Non-Sustainable Development.

Low Carbon is aiming to consult residents on its plan by summer 2027 and then submit it to the Planning Inspectorate by the end of that year.

The Dengie was chosen due to its sunlight exposure, large, flat land and the fact there was an existing electricity grid at the former nuclear power plant.

Pylons that once served the power station could be brought back into use to run the solar farm's energy down to a substation in Rayleigh, explained Ed Perrin, development director at Low Carbon.

"Using infrastructure that is already there is much more preferable to putting in new infrastructure," he said.

Perrin said extensive bird surveys were being carried out to measure the potential impact of the farm.

He also suggested some materials could be delivered by boat during the construction phase, rather than clogging up local roads.

Perrin added: "The scale of our decarbonisation targets in this country and the drive for affordability means projects like this - that are at scale - do need to come forward if we're to hit our targets."

articles.title: Norfolk MP opposing data centre joins government committee
articles.summary: He admits data centres are needed, but he is opposing plans for one in his constituency.
articles.body:
An MP who is opposing plans for a large data centre has admitted the facilities are needed, but does not want one proposed in his constituency built.

Ben Goldsborough, Labour MP for South Norfolk, has been appointed to a new data centre committee, which will scrutinise the government's national policies.

The politician has been vocal in his opposition to plans to build a 150 megawatt (MW) facility in the village of Keswick, near Norwich.

But despite being critical of the bid, Goldsborough insists he is not at odds with his own government's stance on the issue, which wants them built to "power the age of AI".

Data centres were classed as critical national infrastructure by the government last year and it wants to expand capacity to six gigawatts (GW) of continuous capacity by 2030.

Goldsborough will sit on a committee shaping policies around the construction of data centres, and contribute to a National Policy Statement (NPS).

It is currently in its draft form and a consultation has been opened.

The document's foreword currently states: "Britain must build the infrastructure that will power the age of AI, but this government believes how it is built matters just as much as how much we build."

Developers are likely to face expectations that they invest in local communities, create local jobs, and protect local water supplies.

The policies would have important implications for Norfolk, as plans have also been lodged for what would be one of the biggest data centres in the country near King's Lynn .

Goldsborough admitted data centres were needed to "support business, innovation and the technologies of the future".

But he is adamant the Norwich Apex development on the outskirts of the city will be in the wrong place.

He worries about the environmental impact to nearby nature sites and wants heat generated from the site to heat homes.

He said: "What we're seeing with the Keswick one is a mass mega data centre, which is only going to benefit the likes of Elon Musk, Google and others.

"We need data centres which are built in the local interest for local people."

He likened the growth of data centres to a "gold-rush" from private companies and that legislation "hasn't caught up with the times".

However, the developer has insisted it is in a good location and has the potential to boost Norwich's economy .

The site is next to a dual carriageway and the land has been earmarked to become a business park.

It is also close to a substation for a new wind farm off the Norfolk coast.

However, Goldsborough has remained unconvinced, and pointed to a data centre at Norwich Research Park as a good example, saying it has been built in a "mindful way".

He added: "Most importantly it is sovereign data for our research institutions, not a mega data centre which just holds data for whoever pays the highest price."

articles.title: Calls to relax 'Dickensian' Peak District house-buying rules
articles.summary: Anyone wanting to buy an affordable home in the Peak District must have a 10-year connection.
articles.body:
There are calls for Peak District bosses to relax what some locals have called a "Dickensian" housing rule, which they say is hampering efforts to attract and keep young families living and working in the area.

A clause under the national park authority's legally binding planning rules dictates that prospective residents within many areas of the national park need a local connection to the village going back a decade - or a decade within the past 20 years - in order to access affordable housing there.

Several local authorities are calling for the "restrictive" rule to be relaxed amid concerns about sustaining the region's ageing population.

The park authority is now consulting on introducing more flexibility to the rule.

One couple who came up against the rule were Rachel Norman and her partner Billy, who now live in a semi-detached house in Hope with their two young children.

Rachel, 34, says the stress of the process of acquiring their much-loved family home left a lasting impact.

Having grown up in neighbouring Chinley, Rachel left briefly for university in Sheffield before returning to Derbyshire in 2015 to set up a cafe in Hope she now runs with her partner, who is from Matlock.

They spent the majority of the next decade renting in the area while looking for an affordable house to buy.

When one finally came on the market within their price range at the end of 2024, she was told by the national park that her family was blocked from consideration because she fell foul of the 10-year clause by seven months.

"We were very close to 10 years, so we were quite confident with our background of being local people," Rachel said.

"We've got the business and two kids so we've got we've got strong connections there to the local community and we'd been trying to buy a house for nine years... we were like, '[we are] ticking all these boxes, why can't we get it?'."

Areas within the national park such as the Derbyshire Dales have some of the oldest populations in England, with almost three in 10 residents aged 65 or over.

Meanwhile, it is not unusual for schools to have just a handful of children in a class.

The current rule is designed to try to protect housing for local needs and typically applies to new build housing on greenfield sites.

It means an individual or family wishing to occupy an affordable house in Castleton would need to have lived in Castleton, Edale, Hope with Aston, Bradwell or Peak Forest, or any combination of these places for a minimum of 10 years in the past 20 years.

While other national parks have similar policies stipulating a three or five-year connection, the Peak District's is stricter than most.

Rachel and her partner set about filling out an extensive amount of paperwork demonstrating local connection and need, including bank statements, utility bills and evidence of GP registration for each of the past nine-and-a-half years they had lived in the area.

They also submitted a personal letter stressing their local connections, which was signed by a number of local councillors and supporters.

"We said where we've come from, that we live and work here, we've got a local business, you know, we're providing local people with jobs like 10 local people.

"We organise lots of community events, then we just had two young children as well, one who's already at school."

In response, they received what Rachel describes as a "straightforward" email.

"It just said, 'at present, you do not qualify as you do not meet the local qualification provisions'," she said.

Rachel was left with no option but to hope another clause attached to the property would work in their favour. It stipulated that if the house was on the market for three months without any offers, the 10-year requirement would be reduced to five.

"I think because no-one else fit the clause, because it's so restrictive... we got lucky."

The family finally moved in August 2025, but Rachel attributes a shingles diagnosis that summer to the stress of the process.

Phil Mulligan, chief executive of Peak District National Park Authority, said he had sympathy with Rachel, acknowledging the system was "complicated and drawn out".

However, he added the rule was "there for a reason."

"We're in a national park and we are constrained... it is everyone's aspiration to live here, but we can't accommodate all those aspirations," he said.

"What I would ask Rachel to reflect on is, when her children come to an age... will there be any houses for them? Yes, if we maintain these policies."

The stereotypical image of residents of places like the Peak District, home to some of the most picturesque villages in England, are of a resident population typically resistant to change - especially when it comes to housing and adding to its population.

But as the Peak Park authority approaches the final stages of completing a review of its Local Plan, there are plenty of local voices that have emerged calling for it to relax its approach on who gets to live there.

Peter O'Brien, one of the councillors representing Hathersage, where house prices average at about half a million pounds, has been arguing for a relaxation of what he calls a "Dickensian" rule for a number of years.

He says he has seen young people regularly moving away to Chesterfield or Sheffield because of the rule, despite growing up in areas like his.

The Peak District Rural Housing Association, several parish councils such as Hope, Tideswell and Edale, along with High Peak and Derbyshire Dales district council, all put forward concerns about the rule as part of the consultation process for the Peak Park authority's Local Plan review.

Derbyshire Dales District Council told the BBC there was a need to stress "the importance of striking the right balance between protecting local housing opportunities and ensuring communities remain viable in the long term".

High Peak told the consultation that "the current 10-year local connection requirement is too restrictive and should be reduced".

Some parish councils, like Holme Valley, also argued for exceptions to the rule for "essential workers" who do not meet the current criteria but "could be able to carry out essential work within a community, such as community nurses, care workers... currently they are priced out of housing and rentals."

articles.title: Cartel kingpin on FBI’s most wanted list captured in dramatic Mexican military operation
articles.summary: Mexico’s military captured an alleged drug lord listed among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, sparking violent exchanges of gunfire in Sinaloa state on Friday that sent fans fleeing from a baseball game.
articles.body: Mexico’s military captured an alleged drug lord listed among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, sparking violent exchanges of gunfire in Sinaloa state on Friday that sent fans fleeing from a baseball game. Mexico’s defense ministry said Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who leads Guasave-based cartel the Meza-Flores criminal organization, or Los Mazatlecos, was arrested with the help of the US. CNN has approached US authorities for comment. The operation was conducted by “elite military forces” using “stealth and surprise” to reach their target, the ministry posted on X, saying Meza-Flores was taken to Mexico City following his arrest. Meza-Flores is “allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States,” according to an FBI wanted poster offering a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest. He was previously indicted in 2019 for drug trafficking violations and possession of a firearm, and in 2012 for drug trafficking charges, it said. In a 2013 statement, the US Treasury Department said the Meza-Flores cartel had been involved in “an extremely violent turf war” with the rival Sinaloa Cartel – then led by notorious drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, who is now serving time in a US prison. The operation to capture Meza-Flores sparked violent clashes on Friday between the Mexican military and armed militants in Guasave, an area known as the agricultural heart of Mexico. The defense ministry said that authorities “came under attack with gunfire and explosives” upon initiating the operation, and that militants set up roadblocks in several municipalities near the arrest site. Dramatic footage, verified by CNN, shows a barrage of rapid fire from what appear to be Mexican security force helicopters firing at the ground and circling over Guasave city. Local authorities confirmed “an attack on federal personnel” in the city. Baseball fans at the Kuroda Park stadium scrambled out of the stands as a barrage of gunfire rang out on Friday night local time, in footage geolocated by CNN. “Get down, duck down, down, down!” one person shouted in the panic as people clambered over barriers and a baby was heard crying off-camera. An official broadcast showed players from Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams fleeing the field mid-game. “It’s being suspended… there’s a situation happening off the field,” the announcers inform viewers on the broadcast. “We wish first and foremost to ask God that everything is OK… there is a national security incident, it may be better for us to go to break now.” The game, part of the 2026 Liga Mexicana – the country’s premier summer professional baseball league – began at 9:30 p.m. EST. A local resident, running errands when the violence erupted, said private hospitals had been taken over by armed individuals, and businesses including convenience stores and gas stations were being set on fire. “I had to take shelter inside some shops that pulled down their security shutters well before closing time,” he told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity. “People are still trapped inside. “Just meters away from where I was, a convoy of heavily armed civilians passed by, firing shots.” Sinaloa’s state government urged Guasave residents to stay indoors and avoid traveling on the roads, in a statement late Friday. “Authorities from the Interagency Group have been deployed in an operation to restore order, which will be reported once the security operation concludes,” it added. CNN has contacted a representative for the Mexican federal government, Liga Mexicana, Kuroda Park, and both baseball teams playing at the stadium Friday night for comment.

articles.title: At least four killed, 35 injured in fire at power station in Iraq’s Basra
articles.summary: The blaze erupted at the Hartha power station and spread to nearby houses.
articles.body:
A fire has broken out at a power station in southern Iraq, killing at least four people and injuring 35, according to the Iraqi state media.

The Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported on Saturday that the Civil Defence Directorate had brought the fire under control at the Hartha power station and in neighbouring houses.

Operations at the power station, which has a generating capacity of 800 megawatts, were forced to stop after the blaze.

Footage of the fire shared online shows plumes of smoke and burned-out cars. Crowds of people observing the emergency response could also be seen.

The cause of the fire is yet to be confirmed.

Iraq’s electricity infrastructure has ⁠long struggled with decades of underinvestment, inadequate maintenance and an inability to meet peak demand, particularly during ‌the extremely hot summer months.

Fires and technical failures at substations and power facilities have ‌previously ‌disrupted electricity supplies and caused widespread outages.

articles.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
articles.summary: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
articles.body:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".

A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.

More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," said France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.

Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.

He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas .

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

Although this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.

This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn by 2035 - that has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.

articles.title: 'Look beyond what an image shows': Hindu seer's open letter to Rahul, Priyanka over Shiva-Parvati post
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Hindu seer Swami Paramatmananda Saraswati wrote an open letter to Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, explaining the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Hindu seer Swami Paramatmananda Saraswati wrote an open letter to Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, explaining the spiritual significance of an image depicting Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati in an affectionate embrace that Rahul recently shared on social media.In his letter, the seer said that the traditional depiction of Goddess Parvati sitting on Lord Shiva's lap represents the relationship between Shiva, the possessor of power, and Shakti, the creative power. He said the image carries a deeper philosophical meaning rooted in the Upanishads and Hindu scriptures.Addressing the Congress leaders as "Blessed Rahul-Priyanka", Saraswati said he was unsure what Rahul intended to convey through the image but felt it was important to explain its significance."I understand that you have posted a picture of Mata Parvati sitting in the lap of Bhagawan Shiva. I don’t know what exactly you are trying to convey. However I felt like writing. It’s not just a picture. It has deep significance. It symbolises profound wisdom of Upanishads."What the seer said about Shiva and ShaktiExplaining the symbolism of the image, Saraswati said traditional depictions of Uma-Maheshwara, in which Goddess Parvati is shown seated on Lord Shiva's lap, convey the relationship between the ultimate reality, Brahman, and its creative power, Maya.Describing the philosophical significance, he wrote, "The Absolute Truth Brahman, revealed in Veda/Upanishad is in itself, formless, changeless and free from all actions."Explaining the relationship between Shiva and Shakti, the seer said, "While Pārvatī represents Śakti, referred as, Māyā-(the power of manifestation). Bhagawan Shiva unto whom she owes her existence and manifestation/activities."He further explained that their relationship represents the connection between the possessor of power and the power itself. "Their relationship illustrates Śaktimān (शक्तिमान) and शक्तिः (power), where in Shakti has no independent existence apart from its possessor Shaktiman," he wrote.Referring to the manifestation of the universe, Saraswati said, "The universe manifests within the order of Īśvara thru Maya Upādhi and it is understood as Mithyā (dependent reality), having no existence independent of Brahman-The Absolute Truth."He also referred to the depiction of Ardhanarishvara, in which Shiva and Parvati appear as two halves of a single form, as another representation of this philosophical relationship.Explaining the significance of Parvati sitting on Shiva's lap, he wrote, "The imagery conveys that creative power Maya belongs to Shiva who is independent of it whereas Maya is Not."Emphasising the importance of understanding these representations through Hindu teachings, Saraswati said, "It has its own significance within Hindu tradition. Understanding these representations through the Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā (teacher-disciple tradition) allows us to appreciate the wisdom they carry, beyond what the eyes alone perceive."Why Rahul Gandhi shared the Shiva-Parvati imageRahul Gandhi's post came amid a political exchange with the BJP over his remarks about the relationship between his parents, Sonia Gandhi and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi.Speaking at the launch of his mother's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, in New Delhi on Monday, Rahul recalled how his parents would sit together during family meals, with his mother sitting on his father's lap."there would be Papa, and on Papa's lap, there would be Mama," Rahiul said.Recalling how he viewed the relationship as normal during his childhood, Rahul said he was surprised when he noticed that his friends' parents did not behave similarly."Now, I thought this was a normal thing. So I would go to my friend's house, but their parents wouldn't be sitting on each other's lap, and I'd ask my friend, 'What is going on? Why is your mother not sitting on your father's lap?'""This is what we grew up with," Rahul added."She belonged to my father, and my father belonged to her," the Congress leader said while speaking about his parents' relationship.He also told his mother, "Mummy, Papa loved you, but I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you."The remarks drew criticism from BJP leaders, including Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, who took a swipe at the Congress leader."Sorry, Ma'am, he couldn't spare you the embarrassment even on such a special day of your life. The nation figured it out long ago. Hopefully you'll see it now too; this product is beyond launching and relaunching," Sarma said in a post on X, sharing a video of Rahul's remarks.Rahul subsequently shared the image of Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, accompanied by a message accusing BJP and RSS supporters of being unable to experience love because of fear, anger and hatred."Fear, anger and hatred have woven a web in the hearts of BJP and RSS supporters that stops them from experiencing and expressing love. As a true Hindu, it is my duty to free them from this web, so that they too can start to experience the breathtaking beauty and joy of love and belonging in their lives," he posted on X.The Lok Sabha leader of opposition ended his post with the words "Satyam Shivam Sundaram".Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: As Florida uses robot rabbits to eliminate growing population of Burmese pythons; study reveals when and how these python use trees
articles.summary: In 2025, Florida introduced solar-powered robot rabbits to tackle its growing population of invasive Burmese pythons.
articles.body: In 2025, Florida introduced solar-powered robot rabbits to tackle its growing population of invasive Burmese pythons. Now, a new study has revealed when and how these snakes climb trees, giving wildlife officials another clue to help locate and remove them. Researchers tracked 346 Burmese pythons, including 188 adults and 158 juveniles, in Big Cypress National Preserve between 2017 and 2024. According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the study recorded more than 4,000 habitat data points to understand how the snakes use their surroundings.The findings showed that Burmese pythons mostly stay on the ground, with less than 3% of all sightings involving tree climbing. However, around 17% of juvenile pythons and 14% of adult pythons were spotted climbing trees at least once during the study.Why smaller Burmese pythons climb trees more oftenResearchers found that juvenile pythons were more likely to climb trees than adults. Their smaller size and lighter weight may make it easier for them to move along branches. As a python grows heavier, its likelihood of climbing trees decreases. This means wildlife workers may need to look beyond the ground when searching for smaller invasive snakes.The findings could help improve python removal efforts because the snakes are already difficult to spot in Florida's dense vegetation.How Florida's robot rabbits help detect Burmese pythonsIn 2025, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida introduced solar-powered robotic rabbit decoys to attract Burmese pythons. The robots mimic real prey by producing a heat signature and emitting a scent designed to attract snakes. They are also equipped with AI-powered cameras that monitor the surrounding area and alert officials when a python approaches. A trained removal agent can then be sent to capture the snake.“These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,” the district said.How many Burmese pythons have been removed in FloridaBurmese pythons are not native to Florida and are found in and around the Everglades, where they prey on birds, mammals and other reptiles, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). Florida also organises the annual Florida Python Challenge, a 10-day competition that brings together professional and amateur hunters to capture the invasive snakes. In the 2026 challenge, 907 participants from 30 states, as well as Vietnam and Canada, removed 280 Burmese pythons.Since 2017, contractors working with the FWC and South Florida Water Management District have removed more than 19,000 snakes.The latest study adds to these efforts by showing that although most Burmese pythons remain on the ground, smaller snakes are more likely to climb trees.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Illicit alcohol kills 11, poisons 180 in northeast India’s Manipur state
articles.summary: Manipur’s chief minister orders a probe into the incident, saying those responsible will be arrested and punished.
articles.body:
At least 11 people have died after drinking what authorities suspect was spurious alcohol in northeast India’s Manipur state, prompting an investigation.

More than 180 people, who were believed to have consumed toxic liquor, had been admitted to hospitals in Manipur as of Friday.

According to local media, officials have advised locals who have drunk alcohol from Sugnu town in Manipur in the past week to seek medical evaluation. Meanwhile, the deputy police commissioner has advised people not to drink alcohol of unknown origin.

“Over 180 patients have been admitted in the two hospitals so far, while the death toll has reached 11 in the last 48 hours,” Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said in a statement on Friday.

Illicit alcohol is a lucrative industry in India, attracting customers who are too poor to afford licensed brands. Vendors regularly use chemicals to increase the potency of their alcohol.

Methanol is one of the substances used and can be fatal in doses as low as 60ml. Battery acid has also been found in unregulated alcohol in India.

At least 120 people died in Punjab in 2020 after drinking toxic alcohol.

articles.title: Ex-Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia under probe for posing as lawyer without passing bar
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia, ex-White House press secretary, faces a California State Bar investigation over allegations of falsely presenting herself as a qualified lawyer despite never passing the bar exam in the U.S.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California over allegations that she presented herself as a qualified lawyer despite never passing a bar examination in the United States.The investigation follows a complaint filed in October by Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organisation. The California bar informed the group earlier this month that an investigator and legal adviser had been assigned to examine the allegations.Before joining the Trump administration, Zacharia appeared on several television programmes and described herself as a lawyer. Her LinkedIn profile also listed her as the general counsel of a California-based non-profit organisation. Trump referred to her as an “attorney” when announcing her appointment as White House press secretary.Although Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University with a law degree in 2011, she has not passed the bar examination in California or any other US state, according to The Guardian.Michelle Kuppersmith, director of Campaign for Accountability, questioned Zacharia's repeated claims about her professional credentials.“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” Kuppersmith said.“We’re pleased the California bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating,” she added.Zacharia has rejected the allegations. A spokesperson for her told The Guardian: “These are baseless allegations. This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the state bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing.”Zacharia had earlier defended her use of the term “lawyer”, arguing that it was distinct from “attorney”, which she said referred to someone licensed to practise law. In an email to the newspaper, she cited an American Bar Association Journal article discussing the distinction between the two terms.A spokesperson for the State Bar of California confirmed that it was aware of reports concerning Zacharia, describing her as a non-licensee. However, the spokesperson stressed that an investigation or complaint does not establish that someone has engaged in the unauthorised practice of law or violated state statutes. The bar also said its investigations remain confidential.Campaign for Accountability had urged the regulator to examine whether Zacharia misrepresented her qualifications to the public and determine whether she violated California law.The controversy follows Zacharia's brief tenure as Trump's press secretary. She replaced Karoline Leavitt in mid-October but left the position after five days, making her the shortest-serving person to hold the role. During her first press briefing, she stumbled over some of her remarks and took questions primarily from conservative media outlets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to kill Ukrainian American rapper on its soil
articles.summary: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday.
articles.body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday. The Russian defense attaché has been expelled from Denmark in response, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. Two alleged members of the outlawed Danish gang “Loyal to Familia” have been arrested in connection with the attempted killing, police said. Danish broadcaster DR, citing a court hearing, reported the men are suspected of having been recruited to assassinate ​a Ukrainian rapper ahead of a planned performance. Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested ​the two men shortly before the rapper ​Kyivstoner’s September 25 concert, which was later ⁠cancelled. It was unclear how police identified the two men, who ​were stopped in ​a vehicle ⁠carrying several weapons, or how the investigation expanded to include two other men ​who are not accused of participating ​in ⁠the alleged assassination plot targeting Kyivstoner. However, all four men have been held in custody since September, according to ⁠the ​broadcaster. It was also unclear how ​the Russian intelligence services allegedly recruited the two Danish suspects. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said: “It is a clear illustration of the grave security situation Denmark and Europe find ourselves in. We are facing a Russia under pressure which is acting more aggressively and is more willing to take risks.” The Danes’ announcement came as tensions between Europe and Russia heightened again Friday. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. European Commission ​President Ursula von der Leyen said on Saturday the E.U. ⁠stands in full solidarity with Denmark. “This was an ​attack ⁠on E.U. ‌soil. And it is unacceptable. We stand in full ‌solidarity with Denmark. ‌And with all Member States targeted by Russian ⁠hybrid attacks,” she said in an X post. European Council President António Costa said: “We will not be intimidated. Russia’s tactics and threats will not weaken the European Union’s resolve to continue supporting Ukraine.” The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said on Friday the accusations were not backed ‌with proof.

articles.title: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and U.N. Women chief, dies at 71
articles.summary: JOHANNESBURG — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.
articles.body: JOHANNESBURG — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday. Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021. The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress. Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa’s first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country’s first democratically elected leader. Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa’s struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women’s rights and gender equality. “Mama Phumzile was a distinguished leader of our movement and a dedicated servant of the people. She made history as the first woman to serve as Deputy President of South Africa,” the ANC said in a statement Friday. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres expressed condolences and called her “a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.” “Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka’s fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl,” he said in a statement Friday. U.N. Women said her courage inspired people around the world and her leadership helped shape a global movement. “From her early days as an anti-apartheid activist to becoming South Africa’s first woman Deputy President, and later leading U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021, she devoted her life to justice and equality,” the agency said in a statement. Mlambo-Ngcuka was appointed deputy president during a volatile era in South African politics and for the ruling ANC, which was experiencing infighting and a bruising succession battle. She replaced former Deputy President Jacob Zuma when he was fired after being implicated in a corruption scandal involving an arms deal. Despite her known history as a political activist and experienced lawmaker, her appointment drew criticism over her marriage to Bulelani Ngcuka, the country’s lead prosecutor who was pursuing corruption charges against Zuma. She is survived by her husband and their five children.

articles.title: Demolition notices for buildings in Hebron provoke fear among Palestinians
articles.summary: Palestinians fear forced displacement as Israeli authorities target legally licensed homes in West Bank.
articles.body:
Hebron, Occupied West Bank – Amjad al-Qawasmi stood gazing at the eight-storey residential building he constructed 13 years ago in the heart of Hebron. He struggled to understand how it could be reduced to rubble in a matter of moments.

The building in the southern West Bank is one of two upon which the Israeli army posted demolition notices last Sunday morning, even though both are in Area A, which, under the Oslo Accords, is under full Palestinian control.

The buildings are in the Dairat al-Seer area, in the northwest of Hebron. One contains 25 residential apartments, the other has 40, alongside an adjacent home. The Israeli army has set a one-week deadline for filing objections to the demolition orders.

The Israeli authorities justified the decisions by citing the buildings’ proximity to “Settler Road 35”, despite the structures possessing all the necessary permits from the Palestinian Authority and the Hebron Municipality.

Hebron is divided into a larger area under Palestinian administrative control and a smaller area – housing Israeli settlers – in the centre of the city.

The affected families are living in a state of anxiety, fearing that the demolition orders will be carried out. Meanwhile, the property owners have filed formal objections in an attempt to halt the demolitions.

Al-Qawasmi told Al Jazeera that his building was constructed in 2013 at a cost exceeding 18 million shekels ($5.6m). He, along with his father and brother, had prepared the apartments for occupancy from the ground up, installing all necessary utilities after obtaining the required permits from the Ministry of Local Government.

He explained that he, his brothers, and their families live on the lower floors of the building.

Most of the other apartments were sold to families who have yet to complete their payments; a situation exacerbated by the difficult economic conditions they are facing, such as salary cuts and the ban on most Palestinian workers entering Israel for employment, which has been in effect since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

“Like all the residents of the building, we fear the execution of the demolition order. Although we have hired a lawyer to try to freeze the decision, this is an occupation, anything is possible,” said al-Qawasmi.

The families living in the two buildings have begun packing their essential belongings and clothing into cardboard boxes in anticipation of a potential forced eviction to carry out the demolition. However, they remain uncertain about the fate of their furniture and other possessions, should they not be granted the time to clear out their apartments.

Samer Abu Hadid purchased a plot of land in the area five years ago and built a villa for his eight-member family. The 1,165 square metre property cost an estimated $3m.

Last Sunday morning, he was shocked when Israeli soldiers stormed the villa and served him a demolition notice, granting him a one-week window to file an objection. The order stated that it was a military decision based on “security grounds”.

“I told the officer that the villa is legally licensed and there are no grounds for its demolition. He simply replied, ‘Look at the document carefully, the reasons are security-related ‘ and added that I have one week to file an objection. But what can I possibly do in one week against an already-issued demolition order?” he asked Al Jazeera.

Abu Hadid reached out to local authorities to follow up on the matter, yet he remains deeply concerned that the demolition order might actually be carried out.

“We literally cannot sleep any more; we think about this constantly. We don’t know whether we should move out our furniture and empty the villa, or stay put. Nothing is clear, and we are at a loss as to what to do,” he said.

According to a report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (covering the period from November 2024 to October 2025), Israel targeted 97 Palestinian structures in Area A either through actual demolition or the issuance of demolition orders. This is in addition to 46 structures in Area B, 1,390 in Area C and 240 in occupied East Jerusalem.

The Palestinian Commission Against the Wall and Settlements has documented the issuance of 9,518 demolition or ‘stop-construction’ notices between 2015 and the end of September 2026.

They include 344 notices issued during the first nine months of this year. Hebron governorate tops the list with 2,697 notices issued in the city.

Hebron Municipal Council member Muammar al-Oweiwi told Al Jazeera that the recent demolition notices set a precedent in Hebron by targeting Area A, which should be under the full civil and security control of the Palestinian National Authority. Demolition and stop-construction orders were also issued for a family guesthouse and another building in the Farsh al-Hawa area in Area C.

Al-Oweiwi said that the Hebron Municipality is addressing the matter, in coordination with the property owners’ lawyers, by submitting documentation, including building permits, and pursuing the necessary legal procedures.

He added that the case is now before the Israeli courts; the lawyers requested an immediate stay or freeze on the demolition orders, but Israel has yet to respond.

“The municipality is not merely seeking to freeze the decision, but to have it overturned entirely and to secure official documentation confirming that the demolition of these buildings is unlawful,” he stated.

According to al-Oweiwi, the targeting of the two buildings goes beyond threatening dozens of families with the loss of their homes; it also strikes a blow to the Palestinian investment and construction sectors. The significant investments involved are now jeopardised, undermining investor confidence and threatening the city’s economic and urban stability.

Al-Oweiwi added that the Israeli justification that the buildings are near roads used by settlers is incorrect. He said the structures are within residential neighbourhoods and pose no threat to the roads.

“What is taking place falls within the framework of a policy of collective punishment and pressure on the Palestinians, and an attempt to undermine the citizens’ trust in their national institutions by encroaching upon their jurisdiction in areas that, under signed agreements, are subject to Palestinian administration,” he concluded.

articles.title: Nayib Bukele promised Haiti a ‘triumph.’ Are his forces delivering?
articles.summary: Gun-toting robots trotting down a dark alley. The blaze of a helicopter-launched rocket. A gang boss’s mansion crumbling in the sunshine. No one does video like Nayib Bukele.
articles.body: Gun-toting robots trotting down a dark alley. The blaze of a helicopter-launched rocket. A gang boss’s mansion crumbling in the sunshine. Thousands of Salvadoran troops landed in Haiti last month to combat gangs overrunning the Caribbean nation. While it’s too early to tell if they’re succeeding, the personal involvement of popular Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has stirred rare hope on the island – and avid interest across Latin America. What’s the difference between the newly arrived Salvadorans and all the other fighting forces in Haiti’s crowded security landscape? “They’re really good at making videos,” one local security source said. Most of what we know about the Salvadoran force has come in glimpses from Bukele’s social media accounts. The deal governing their presence has not been made public, but the 45-year-old president is effectively drumming up support with promises in Creole to root out the gangs as he has done in El Salvador, combined with explosive footage and online banter. “For the first time, I felt like someone had listened to me,” said Sophia Fecu, describing the moment she saw a video posted by Bukele that showed helicopters attacking gang leader Lanmo Sanjou’s house on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince. “I felt like my voice had finally been heard.” Days earlier, Fecu, a Haitian entrepreneur and writer, had posted a picture of the notorious gang clubhouse on X and tagged Bukele. “I just felt that it wasn’t right for these criminals to be living so comfortably while the rest of the population was forced to flee their homes and communities,” she said from the US, where she now lives. “I honestly didn’t expect him to respond.” But he did. Bukele answered on X asking for the location of the house, sparking a flurry of responses. Three days later, he posted an update: Video of helicopters blasting apart the building’s blue-tiled facade, shadowy figures of suspected gang members fleeing the compound on foot. It’s hard to imagine other forces in Haiti crowdsourcing coordinates for a well-known gang headquarters. But Haitian police, a secretive task force involving a private military contractor led by Erik Prince, and the multinational Gang Suppression Force have been busy, too: Police announced on Thursday that they had killed 34 gang members in a major operation in the Port-au-Prince neighborhood of Martissant. The GSF, still building its force, said its operations are entering a “new phase” of pressure and is also posting more videos of soldiers at work. But no one boasts the same reach as Bukele. Some friction was inevitable. Security sources in Haiti complain about a lack of cooperation and credit-sharing with the Salvadorans and point out that fighting videos don’t show the difficult reality of working in Haiti, like finding parts to repair helicopters damaged by gang fire. Last week, Salvadoran troops reportedly fired perilously close to GSF troops. On another occasion, they sparked tensions after trying to enter a GSF outpost without notice, sources said. On Friday, two soldiers died and two others were wounded in an incident handling explosive material, according to the Salvadoran army. Still, there is hope for a deeper eventual collaboration once the new force finds its footing. And Bukele will need it. He has raised expectations in an exhausted nation, and now he must deliver. His troops are far from home and facing a gang alliance that knows the terrain better, can replace fallen soldiers with forced conscripts, and shares information and resources across Port-au-Prince. “Imagine if the police, task force, GSF and Salvadorans were all working together, with their combined ground and air forces — that would be amazing,” a security source said wistfully.

articles.title: Ukraine deals major blow to Putin’s Crimea lifeline, European intel assessment claims
articles.summary: Gen. Philip Breedlove says cutting the Kerch Bridge will severely damage Russia's ability to resupply Crimea as Kyiv lands three strikes in four days.
articles.body: Ukraine's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prized infrastructure projects, have dealt a potentially significant blow to Moscow's military supply routes into occupied Crimea, raising questions about Russia's ability to sustain operations as both sides prepare for a difficult winter. A European intelligence assessment dated Nov. 18 and obtained by Fox News Digital describes Ukraine's latest assault as likely its most successful attack on the heavily defended crossing, following a coordinated campaign targeting Russian air defenses, radar and electronic warfare systems. Ret. Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital the consequences could extend far beyond the destruction of a symbolic Russian landmark. "The Russians are extremely limited in how they get supplies to Crimea and cutting the Kerch bridge will severely, severely damage their ability to resupply Crimea," Breedlove said. UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY' What happened to the bridge? On Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones struck the 12-mile bridge linking Russia's Krasnodar region to Crimea, collapsing a major section of the roadway into the Kerch Strait and damaging the adjacent railway. The crossing, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, has served as both a critical transportation link and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014. According to the European intelligence assessment, the attack followed a multiweek Ukrainian operation against Russian defensive systems, intended to weaken the bridge's protection before the main strike. Ukraine subsequently struck the railway again on Nov.19, temporarily halting train traffic and bringing the number of attacks to three in four days. The damage has disrupted one of Russia's most direct supply connections to Crimea, which Moscow uses to support military operations in southern Ukraine. PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE Why it matters militarily Russia has developed an alternative land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, but the European intelligence assessment warns that shifting additional military supplies onto those roads could create significant vulnerabilities. The assessment identifies slower transportation routes, exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks and pressure on other logistical infrastructure as potential consequences. Breedlove said Ukraine's campaign should be viewed as an attempt to weaken Russia's hold on the peninsula, rather than simply destroy a bridge. He argued that Russia's options are further constrained by Ukraine's success in challenging Russian naval power in the northern Black Sea. He pointed out that Ukraine has used maritime and aerial drones to push back Russia's Black Sea Fleet despite lacking large conventional warships. The European assessment also warns that repairing the bridge could take months. Although limited road traffic might resume within weeks, replacing the collapsed section could take considerably longer, particularly if Ukrainian attacks continue. Damage above the Kerch–Yenikale Canal could also disrupt shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS Who is gaining momentum? Despite Ukraine's success in striking the bridge, a European intelligence source familiar with Russian strategic assessments offered a pessimistic view of the broader conflict. "It has more symbolic meaning, but also logistics is paralyzed right now," the source told Fox News Digital, describing the immediate impact of the attacks. However, the source warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its winter offensive while using negotiations with Washington to increase political pressure on Kyiv. "The general trend is not good for Ukraine," the source said. According to the source, Russia believes it can sustain military pressure long enough to force Ukraine into territorial concessions, particularly in the east. "They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source said, describing Moscow's expectations. Breedlove strongly disputed the assessment that Russia was gaining the upper hand militarily. "Militarily, the tide is turning against Russia," Breedlove told Fox News Digital, arguing that Russian forces have suffered staggering casualties while making limited battlefield gains. He said Russian losses in recent months had been extraordinarily high and argued that Moscow's military was failing to achieve significant territorial advances. Breedlove did, however, acknowledge a distinction between military momentum and the political pressure facing Ukraine. He suggested that changes in Washington's approach to negotiations could strengthen Putin's position even if Russian forces were struggling on the battlefield. The competing assessments highlight a central question facing Ukraine: whether its military successes can translate into greater diplomatic leverage before Russia's winter offensive intensifies. UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA What happens next? Putin has threatened retaliation over the bridge attacks, and on Friday Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault against Ukrainian cities, killing at least eight people, according to Ukrainian authorities. The strikes came hours after Putin appeared alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China, as Washington continued efforts to advance peace negotiations. The European intelligence assessment warns that further Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge during repairs are highly likely, potentially prolonging disruptions to Russian supplies. For Kyiv, keeping it vulnerable offers a way to increase the cost of Russia's occupation while demonstrating that even Putin's most heavily defended infrastructure remains within reach.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Half of California's DAs sue Newsom over death row clemency
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom faces a lawsuit from 29 district attorneys and victims' families who say his mass clemency for 548 death row inmates skipped victim notice.
articles.body: District attorneys in half of California's 58 counties have signed onto a lawsuit alongside victims' families and law enforcement groups against term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom over his lame-duck move to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates in the Golden State. Many of the prosecutors had publicly condemned the governor's move shortly after he announced it earlier this month. "Only this Court can stop the Governor’s disregard of the law — his abuse of power," former Sacramento District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert wrote in the 58-page petition, filed Monday. "His eleventh-hour decision to grant commutation en masse intentionally disregarded the statutorily required notice to the victims of these heinous crimes and the prosecutors who obtained those convictions and penalties, and it even interfered with this Court’s mandatory duty to meaningfully review his decisions." Schubert, who said she worked through the weekend on the filing, is the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which is spearheading the lawsuit on behalf of 29 district attorneys and the families of more than two dozen victims. MICHAEL RUIZ: CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS REVOLT AFTER NEWSOM ORDERS STATE'S WORST KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW The Governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false. Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped at knifepoint from a slumber party at her mother's house and strangled to death in 1993, is among the petitioners. Polly's killer, Richard Allen Davis, has been on death row since 1996. Other victims' families include those of slain 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, Placer County Sheriff's Detective Mike Davis, Pittsburg Police Officer Larry Lasater, Sacramento Deputy Danny Paul Oliver, and five U.S. Forest Service firefighters killed battling the 40,000-acre Esperanza Fire in 2006 — among others. articles.body: Former Italian police chief Gianni De Gennaro has died at the age of 78, the government announced on Saturday, with Italian media reporting that he had died by suicide.De Gennaro, who served as Italy's police chief from 2000 to 2007, was under investigation on suspicion of obstructing a fresh probe into the mafia.Alfredo Mantovano, an official at the Italian Prime Minister's Office, expressed shock over his death, describing De Gennaro as a public servant whose qualities, sense of duty and commitment to institutions he greatly admired.De Gennaro was found dead at his country home after relatives raised the alarm when they were unable to reach him, according to media reports. Italian outlets, including La Repubblica, Corriere della Sera and ANSA, reported that he had shot himself.Less than a week before his death, prosecutors in Caltanissetta, Sicily, had named the former police chief in an investigation into alleged attempts to obstruct inquiries into the 1992 mafia bombing in Palermo that killed anti-mafia magistrate Paolo Borsellino and five members of his security detail.Prosecutors had sought house arrest for De Gennaro. He denied any wrongdoing, and no court had ruled on the allegations.Who was Gianni De GennaroGianni De Gennaro was a prominent figure in Italy's fight against organised crime, with a career spanning the investigation of the Sicilian mafia, senior police leadership and intelligence services.He worked closely with anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone during landmark investigations in the 1980s and helped oversee the extradition of mafia turncoat Tommaso Buscetta from Brazil.De Gennaro later headed the Anti-Mafia Investigative Directorate (DIA), served as Italy's national police chief from 2000 to 2007, and went on to lead the country's intelligence coordination department.His tenure as police chief was also marked by controversy over the security operation during the 2001 Group of Eight (G8) summit in Genoa, where violent clashes broke out between police and anti-globalisation protesters. De Gennaro denied personal wrongdoing and was ultimately acquitted in a related case.In 2013, he became chairman of state-controlled aerospace and defence group Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo, and held the position until 2020.(with Reuters inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: Navy's Fleet Air Arm: From tracking enemy radars in 1965 to monitoring China along LAC
articles.summary: When the Indian Navy's Fleet Air Arm is discussed, the focus is usually on submarines, ships and sea lines of communication.
articles.body: When the Indian Navy's Fleet Air Arm is discussed, the focus is usually on submarines, ships and sea lines of communication. But naval aviation has also played a less-publicised role over land, supporting the Army and the Air Force with intelligence and surveillance. That capability dates back to the 1965 war and has now returned along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), where the Navy's P-8I long-range maritime reconnaissance aircraft are helping monitor Chinese activity.The precedent was set by the French-built Breguet Alizé, an anti-submarine warfare aircraft operated by the Navy in the 1960s. It carried a belly-mounted radar and an ARAR 11-D Electronic Support Measures (ESM) suite, with eight antennae providing 360-degree coverage. The system could passively detect radar emissions and help locate their sources.The Air Force recognised that the capability could also be used to detect ground-based radars. Following the 1962 war with China, an Alizé was deployed to identify Chinese radar stations along the LAC, according to a United Services Institution publication.The aircraft's most notable mission came during the 1965 war with Pakistan. Radar installations at Sakesar and Badin had begun guiding Pakistani fighters towards Indian aircraft, prompting the IAF to seek the Navy's help.An Alizé commanded by Lieutenant Sourirajulu Ramsagar was moved to Agra before operating out of Ambala. It flew four missions over the western sector, covering the border stretch from Pathankot to Jamnagar at an altitude of around 15,000 feet.The aircraft deliberately allowed Pakistani radars to track it while its ESM equipment picked up their emissions. The crew plotted and triangulated the sources, identified eight radar installations and relayed their coordinates to the Air Force. Canberra photo-reconnaissance aircraft subsequently refined the data, which was used to plan strikes.From Alizé to P-8IThe capability has evolved with the Boeing 737-based P-8I, equipped with advanced sensors for maritime reconnaissance, anti-submarine warfare and electronic intelligence.During the 2017 Doklam standoff, P-8I aircraft were deployed to monitor Chinese People's Liberation Army movements in the Chumbi Valley. The deployment was subsequently confirmed by former Chief of Defence Staff General Bipin Rawat.The Navy's support along the LAC has since become more regular. During the 2020 eastern Ladakh standoff, P-8I aircraft and Sea Guardian drones were deployed at the Army's request to monitor Chinese troop movements and infrastructure along the border.The aircraft and drones supplemented satellite imagery and other unmanned systems, providing live feeds and electro-optical imagery to aid operational decisions. Their surveillance covered Ladakh in the western sector as well as Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh in the east.The Navy's role in joint operations was also visible during Exercise Poorvi Prahar in November 2024, when the three services conducted drills in the Eastern Theatre. The P-8I participated in exercises involving intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance, mobilisation and logistics in mountainous terrain.The Fleet Air Arm's role, therefore, extends well beyond India's coastline. Its sensors, electronic intelligence capabilities and surveillance feeds can help the Army monitor activity across difficult terrain, adding to intelligence gathered through ground-based systems, satellites and Air Force assets.While operational details remain classified, the evolution from the Alizé tracking Pakistani radar emissions in 1965 to the P-8I monitoring activity along the Himalayas underscores the Navy's growing role in India's joint military and intelligence architecture.
