articles.body: A great-grandfather from Busselton, Western Australia, has discovered that he won more than $650,000 in Saturday Lotto after spending several weeks ignoring calls from an unfamiliar number. The man, who is in his 70s, had been so occupied with caring for his 91-year-old mother that he initially failed to recognise the importance of the messages from Lotterywest. His unexpected windfall came from a ticket purchased online, and he is now planning a special family gathering to share the news with 5 generations of relatives.Great-grandfather wins over $650,000 after missing Lotterywest callsThe unexpected lottery win followed a busy period in the man's life, during which his main responsibility was looking after his elderly mother. According to PerthNow, the Busselton resident had been receiving calls from an unfamiliar number for approximately two weeks but repeatedly chose not to answer them.When he eventually picked up a call from Lotterywest, he still did not realise what the organisation was trying to tell him. His attention remained focused on his mother's care, leaving him with little time to properly listen to the caller.The man later explained that he had initially brushed off the conversation because he was occupied with looking after his mother. The Lotterywest representative asked him to return the call, but he promptly forgot about the request.It was only when Lotterywest managed to contact him again that he began to understand the significance of the message. What had initially seemed like an ordinary missed call turned out to be news of a substantial lottery prize.A birthday-number ticket brought an unexpected windfallThe great-grandfather's winning entry was purchased online for $6.60 as a System 7 ticket. He had selected numbers based on birthdays, a familiar approach among lottery players who prefer using personally meaningful dates instead of random numbers.The ticket secured him a total of $652,714, including prizes from other divisions. The win came in the Saturday Lotto draw held on August 22, 2026, in which he was one of 10 division one winners across Australia.PerthNow reported that the winning numbers were 9, 11, 2, 1, 13 and 20, while the supplementary numbers were 28 and 45.Despite the significant amount involved, the winner did not immediately share the news with his wider family. He had kept the information largely private, with his 91-year-old mother being the only relative who knew about this fortune.The delayed discovery also meant that the prize announcement came more than 2 weeks after the draw. While many winners might immediately celebrate such news, his reaction was shaped by the responsibilities that had occupied his attention throughout the period.His mother will be part of the first celebrationHis mother, who is 91, already knows about the win, and the pair planned a Chinese takeaway to mark the occasion. The choice is particularly meaningful because she enjoys Chinese food, making it a simple celebration centred on something she likes.According to PerthNow, the man regularly takes part in family gatherings that bring together five generations. These occasions provide an opportunity for relatives of different ages to spend time together, and he sees the next gathering as the right moment to reveal his lottery success.Lotterywest explains why birthday numbers remain popularThe draw also offered an insight into the number choices that many lottery players make. Lotterywest spokeswoman Jennie Fitzhardinge told PerthNow that numbers associated with birthdays and other significant dates are commonly selected by people who choose their own entries.She explained that lower numbers often feature more prominently in division one winning combinations because many players use birthdays and personally important dates when filling out their tickets.The August 22 draw produced 3 division one winners in Western Australia, including the Busselton great-grandfather. The remaining winners were part of the 10 division one prize recipients recorded nationally.After finally learning about the money, his attention has turned towards sharing the moment with the people closest to him. His planned family meal will give five generations a chance to celebrate together.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders met in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys to discuss Ukraine.

That meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

An unforgettable trip to England Sometimes vacations don’t go as planned. American sisters Jan and Jill Shropshire discovered this the hard way on a trip to the English Midlands in 1997. A mistake with the key led to Jill accidentally locking the pair of them inside their room in a countryside B&B in a converted old house. Then when they tried to summon help, they realized they were all alone in the building. They survived their ordeal and were eventually rescued, with thanks to some peanut butter, a free-standing sink and some helpful Russians. An ancient superpower Operating out of the rugged landscape of what is modern-day central Turkey, the Hittites were a powerhouse empire some 3,500 years ago. They raided Babylon, built an awesome fleet of armored chariots and squared up against legendary Egyptian pharaohs like Ramesses the Great. They’ve been largely forgotten by popular history, but are now back in the headlines thanks to a startling discovery at Šamuḫa, an ancient dig site in central Turkey. Archaeologists recently unearthed a stash of cuneiform-inscribed clay tablets, which offer an intimate, and occasionally strange, peek into everyday life 35 centuries ago. Diego Arellan said he had never encountered transgender ideology until he moved to the United States from Peru as a teenager. "I started hanging out with a lot of people that were living that lifestyle and that also recommended me to live that lifestyle because [of] the way I acted," Arellan told Fox News Digital. Everything that I'm seeing out there, like in social media, or anywhere I go I see, like this is a way you have to go in order for you to feel fulfilled, at least because I always struggle with my identity,'" he continued. PRISHA MOSLEY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME "I transitioned when I was 18 and a lot of things happened during that season just because I was very immature in that season … I went through a lot [of] gender dysphoria," Arellan said. He went on to describe what he said were side effects of the hormone pills he took, saying his body was reacting to something that was "not natural." "[I had] a lot of like, pain on my body and just changes, but I still went through it because I really thought that this was gonna be the path that was gonna make me happy … There was a lot of rejection as well from the people I start[ed] dating … I was lying not only to me, but I was lying to the people out there who thought they were dating any other woman, but in reality, [I] was not," he continued. WOMAN WHO LIVED AS MAN SAYS SHE GRIEVED ‘UNWANTED BODY PARTS’ AFTER TRANSITION "There was a lot of confusion, a lot of stress, a lot like just also wanting to kill myself at one point because of all these things I was building and thinking that this was the right path again," Arellan added. Arellan said he had breast augmentation surgery, a Brazilian butt lift and Botox injections in different areas of his face. "It was turning into an addiction because it was never enough. articles.body: A Purdue University professor, her husband and their two teenage daughters were found dead inside their home in West Lafayette, Indiana, after one of the girls reportedly called 911 to warn that her father was threatening to shoot the family. The victims were identified as Dr Julie Tkach, 53, her husband Thomas Tkach, 51, and their daughters Katharyn Tkach, 17, and Lauren Tkach, 16, according to the Tippecanoe County Coroner's Office. Julie was a clinical assistant professor in hospitality and tourism management at Purdue University. Thomas worked for the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office.The family was discovered at their residence on Thursday, November 19. Authorities had been alerted to the incident after receiving information about four people found dead inside the house.According to emergency dispatch audio obtained by Star City TV, one of the daughters had contacted authorities before the shooting. In the recording, a dispatcher can be heard telling responding officers that the caller's father had a gun and was threatening to shoot the family. "She advised that her father had a gun and was threatening to shoot the family," the dispatcher said, adding that multiple gunshots were heard before the telephone line went silent.The alarming recording captured the moments when authorities lost contact with the teenager.What investigators foundThe Tippecanoe County Coroner's Office ruled the deaths a murder-suicide. Preliminary autopsy findings determined that Julie, Katharyn and Lauren died from multiple gunshot wounds, with all three deaths classified as homicides. Thomas died from a gunshot wound to the head, which was ruled a suicide. Toxicology results were still pending.Indiana State Police authorities have not disclosed what prompted the shooting or established a motive.Purdue professor remembered by colleaguesJulie had joined Purdue University in 2024. Before that, she taught at South Dakota State University, where she was named Teacher of the Year for the 2021-22 academic year by the College of Education and Human Sciences.Purdue University expressed grief over the deaths in a statement. "We are saddened by this tragedy and the death of Julie and her family. We offer our condolences and support to her colleagues, peers, students and all who are affected," a university spokesperson said.Norah Ashcraft, a victim services coordinator with the Lafayette Police Department, shared a message following the family's deaths.In a Facebook post, she thanked people who had supported the family, particularly the two girls, through everyday interactions and acts of kindness. Ashcraft drew attention to the issue of domestic violence, writing that one of its most devastating aspects was that people often did not get an opportunity to reach out to those experiencing abuse before a tragedy occurred. articles.title: Israeli attacks on Gaza kill at least four Palestinians
articles.summary: Israeli drone attack kills three people in Gaza City, another shot dead by Israeli forces in Jabalia.
articles.body:
Israeli attacks in Gaza have killed at least four Palestinians in violation of last year’s “ceasefire”, as winter flooding deepens the humanitarian crisis in the enclave.

At least three people were killed when the car they were travelling in was struck by an Israeli drone on Saturday in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. Separately, a Palestinian man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Halawa displacement camp, east of northern Gaza’s Jabalia refugee camp.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire”, which came into force last October.

The ongoing attacks on the enclave coincide with a surge in pogroms carried out by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Late on Friday, Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was shot dead by security guards from an illegal Israeli settlement near the village of Dura al-Qar, north of Ramallah.

The Palestinian Health Ministry said his body was being withheld by Israeli authorities. Another Palestinian man was detained during the incident.

Reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers have been carrying out attacks with “impunity”.

“Less than 3 percent of Israeli attacks that are investigated lead to a partial or full conviction by Israeli authorities. Also, the number of settler attacks reported to Israeli authorities is very, very low because Palestinians are often detained, questioned or harassed for filing reports against violent settlers,” Odeh reported.

The violence inflicted on Palestinians in the West Bank has been condemned by Israeli allies, including the United Kingdom. Critics say Western leaders have not supported their rhetoric with sufficient action.

Earlier this month, an Al Jazeera investigation found that the UK had awarded $14.4m in new public contracts to firms with links to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, despite recently announcing a ban on importing goods from such settlements.

The British government has also sanctioned companies involved in settlement expansion.

Winter weather has compounded the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, with the World Food Programme (WFP) warning earlier this week that Palestinians have been forced to burn rubbish to cook their food.

“Now even the rubbish is wet,” warned Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director for Palestine.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said that more than 100,000 tents in Egypt cannot be delivered to Gaza due to strict conditions imposed by Israel.

“Usually anything under 38 millimetres is okay; anything above, it’s usually deemed as not acceptable,” Hughes explained.

“It is not a statement of dual use; it is just that this tent at this time is not allowed to enter Gaza … We don’t get the specifics,” said Karl Baker, head of the IOM’s Gaza programme.

Gaza’s Health Ministry reported on Saturday that 1,671 people had been killed since the “ceasefire” came into effect last October.

Meanwhile, 74,736 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.
